title: How your body gets rid of waste: kidneys, breath and sweat

summary.text: Your body makes waste that must leave, and kidneys give most of it back to the body first. How can a filter do that? In this unit you will find your kidneys, test what three different filters hold back, and play a sorting game on how waste leaves.
summary.art: A child drinking water from a steel tumbler, with a see-through view of two bean-shaped kidneys in her lower back joined by two thin tubes to a small bladder.

intro.hook: You drink clear water, pale buttermilk and brown tea. Yet your urine is always some shade of yellow. Where does the yellow come from, and what else is leaving with it?
intro.text: Urine is made from your blood, by your two kidneys. The yellow is a waste left over when old red blood cells are broken down. Urine also carries a waste called urea, which your body makes when it uses protein. Your lungs and your skin remove waste too. In this unit you find your kidneys with your thumbs. Then you pour salty tea with flour in it through three filters. You find out what a filter can hold back, and what the kidneys must do after filtering.
intro.art: A steel tumbler of water, a tumbler of buttermilk and a tumbler of tea in a row, with an arrow leading to a question mark coloured pale yellow.

outcomes: I can name the wastes my cells make, and say why they must leave my body.
I can name the three main ways out for waste, and say what leaves by each.
I can find where my kidneys are, and trace the path of urine from kidney to bladder.
I can explain how a filter sorts things by size, and what the kidney's filters hold back.
I can explain how the kidneys take back what the body needs, and why this removes unknown wastes.
I can test three filters fairly and say what my results show.
I can explain what urine is made of, and why its colour and amount change.
I can explain what happens when kidneys stop working, and how dialysis and a transplant help.

terms.meaning: Something a cell has made or has left over, which the body cannot use and must send out.
terms.example: Carbon dioxide and urea are wastes. Your cells make them all day and all night.
terms.art: A round cell with small arrows leaving it, labelled carbon dioxide and urea.

terms.meaning: Sending out the wastes that the body's own cells have made.
terms.example: Breathing out carbon dioxide is excretion. Passing urine is excretion too.
terms.art: A child with three arrows leaving her body: one from the nose, one from the skin and one from low in the belly.

terms.meaning: A gas that cells make when they use food for energy. Blood carries it to the lungs.
terms.example: Every breath you blow out carries carbon dioxide away.
terms.art: A child breathing out, with a small cloud labelled CO2 leaving her mouth.

terms.meaning: A waste that the liver makes when the body breaks down protein. It dissolves in water.
terms.example: After a meal with dal or egg, your liver makes more urea. Your kidneys send it out.
terms.art: A liver with small dots leaving it into a blood vessel that leads to a kidney.

terms.meaning: One of two organs in your lower back that clean the blood and make urine.
terms.example: Each of your kidneys is about the size of your fist. A kidney is shaped like a rajma bean.
terms.art: Two bean-shaped kidneys, one on each side of a backbone, just below the ribs.

terms.meaning: Something with small holes. It lets small things pass and holds back things bigger than the holes.
terms.example: A tea strainer is a filter. It lets the tea pass and holds back the leaves.
terms.art: A tea strainer over a tumbler, with tea flowing through and leaves staying in the strainer.

terms.meaning: One of the tiny cleaning units in a kidney. Each has a filter and a long thin tube.
terms.example: Each of your kidneys has about a million nephrons, all working side by side.
terms.art: A single nephron drawn large: a small ball inside a cup, joined to a long winding tube.

terms.meaning: The filter of a nephron. It is a tiny ball of very thin blood vessels with holes in their walls.
terms.example: Water, salt, sugar and urea pass through the glomerulus. Blood cells are too big to pass.
terms.art: A tiny ball of looped blood vessels inside a cup, with small dots passing out and large red discs staying in.

terms.meaning: To take something back. The tube of a nephron reabsorbs water, salt and sugar into the blood.
terms.example: Your kidneys reabsorb about 99 of every 100 parts of the liquid they filter.
terms.art: A winding tube with arrows going from inside the tube back into a blood vessel wrapped around it.

terms.meaning: The liquid the kidneys make from blood. It is water with urea, salts and other wastes dissolved in it.
terms.example: Urine is about 95 parts water in every 100. The other 5 parts are wastes and salts.
terms.art: A drop of pale yellow liquid, drawn large, with tiny dots labelled urea and salt inside it.

terms.meaning: A thin tube that carries urine from a kidney down to the bladder. You have two.
terms.example: Urine trickles down your two ureters all day, a few drops at a time.
terms.art: Two kidneys with two thin tubes running down to a bag below them.

terms.meaning: A stretchy bag low in your belly that stores urine until you go to the toilet.
terms.example: When your bladder is about half full, it signals your brain. You feel the need to go.
terms.art: A round stretchy bag low in a child's belly, half filled with pale yellow liquid.

terms.meaning: A tiny coiled tube in the skin that makes sweat and sends it out through a pore.
terms.example: You have about 2 to 4 million sweat glands. Many are on your palms, soles and forehead.
terms.art: A cut through skin showing one coiled tube deep down, with a straight duct rising to a pore on the surface.

terms.meaning: A treatment that cleans the blood with a machine when the kidneys cannot do it.
terms.example: A person on dialysis usually spends about four hours on the machine, three times a week.
terms.art: A woman resting in a chair beside a machine, with two thin tubes running between her arm and the machine.

explanations.concept: Your cells make waste all the time
explanations.definition: Excretion is sending out the wastes that the body's own cells have made. A waste is something the cells cannot use.
explanations.description: Every cell in your body is at work. A cell takes in sugar and oxygen and uses them for energy. This leaves carbon dioxide and water. A cell also uses protein to build and repair itself. When protein is broken down, a poison called ammonia is left over. Your liver quickly changes ammonia into urea, which is far less harmful. Your body also gets more water and more salt than it needs on some days. All of these must leave. If they stayed, they would build up in your blood and make you very ill within days. Stools are a different matter. Most of a stool is food that was never digested, with gut bacteria and water. That food passed through the tube of your gut and never entered your cells. One part of a stool is true waste. It is the brown colour, which your liver made from old red blood cells.
examples: Carbon dioxide: made in every cell that uses food for energy.
Urea: made in the liver from the leftovers of protein.
Extra water and extra salt: what you took in beyond what you need.
Colour wastes: made when old red blood cells are broken down.
explanations.art: A large cell with sugar and oxygen going in, and carbon dioxide, water and a small dot labelled ammonia coming out.

explanations.concept: There are three main ways out
explanations.definition: Waste leaves the body through the lungs, the kidneys and the skin. The blood carries each waste to its way out.
explanations.description: Blood flows past every cell and picks up the wastes. Then the blood takes them to three organs. The lungs remove carbon dioxide, which is a gas, and you breathe it out. The kidneys remove wastes that dissolve in water, such as urea and extra salt, and send them out in urine. The skin lets out sweat, which is water with a little salt and a very little urea. The liver helps all three. It changes poisons into forms that the kidneys can remove, and it sends colour wastes into the gut. The kidneys do the largest share of the cleaning. Sweat is mainly for cooling you, and it carries out only a small amount of waste.
examples: Lungs: carbon dioxide and some water, in every breath.
Kidneys: urea, extra salt, extra water and many other dissolved wastes.
Skin: water, a little salt and a very little urea, in sweat.
Liver: makes urea, and sends colour wastes out through the gut.
explanations.art: A child's body outline with the lungs, the two kidneys and the skin highlighted, and an arrow leaving from each.

explanations.concept: Where your kidneys are, and how blood reaches them
explanations.definition: The kidneys are two bean-shaped organs in the lower back. They lie one on each side of the backbone, just under the lowest ribs.
explanations.description: Put your hands on your waist with your thumbs on your back. Slide your hands up until your thumbs touch your lowest ribs. Your kidneys lie under your thumbs. Each kidney is about the size of your own fist. A thick blood vessel brings blood into each kidney. About one fifth of all the blood your heart pumps goes to the kidneys. That is a large share for two small organs. Cleaned blood leaves each kidney by another vessel. The urine leaves by a thin tube called a ureter. The two ureters lead down to the bladder, which is low in your belly. From the bladder, a short tube called the urethra leads outside.
examples: A kidney is shaped like a rajma bean. In English, rajma is called the kidney bean.
An adult's kidney is about 11 centimetres long. A child's kidney is smaller, about the size of the child's fist.
Your lowest ribs cover the top part of each kidney and help to protect it.
explanations.art: A child seen from behind with hands on her waist and thumbs on her back, and the two kidneys drawn under the thumbs.

explanations.concept: Step one: the kidney filters the blood by size
explanations.definition: Each kidney has about a million nephrons. A nephron begins with a filter called a glomerulus. It lets small particles out of the blood and holds back large ones.
explanations.description: A glomerulus is a tiny ball of very thin blood vessels. Their walls have holes far too small to see, even with a school microscope. The heart's push presses the blood against these walls. Water passes through the holes. So does everything small that is dissolved in the water: salt, sugar, urea and many others. Red blood cells and white blood cells are too big, so they stay in the blood. Large proteins stay too. The liquid that passes through is called the filtrate. It looks like pale water, and it collects in a cup around the ball. The filter sorts only by size. It lets useful sugar through as easily as harmful urea. An adult's kidneys filter about 180 litres of liquid a day in this way.
examples: Passes the filter: water, salt, sugar, urea.
Held back: red blood cells, white blood cells, large proteins.
A tea strainer works the same way. It holds back leaves and lets the dissolved tea through.
explanations.art: A ball of thin looped blood vessels inside a cup, with tiny dots passing through the walls into the cup and large red discs staying inside the vessels.

explanations.concept: Step two: the kidney takes back what the body needs
explanations.definition: To reabsorb is to take back. The long tube of each nephron reabsorbs water, salt and sugar from the filtrate and returns them to the blood.
explanations.description: The filtrate flows from the cup into a long, thin, winding tube. Blood vessels wrap around the tube. The cells in the tube's wall have pumps that grip particular particles and carry them back to the blood. One kind of pump carries sugar. Another carries salt. Water follows the salt. In a healthy person, all the sugar is taken back. So is nearly all the water and salt. About 99 of every 100 parts of the filtrate return to the blood. Urea has no pump that returns all of it, so much of it stays in the tube. The tube also pushes a few extra wastes straight into the liquid. What reaches the end of the tube is urine. This way of working has one great strength. The kidney does not have to recognise a waste. Anything small that is not taken back leaves the body. That is how you get rid of a new medicine that your body has never met before.
examples: Taken back fully: sugar.
Taken back as needed: water and salt.
Left in the tube: much of the urea, extra salt, extra water, used medicines.
Of 180 litres filtered in a day, an adult passes only about 1 and a half litres as urine.
explanations.art: A long winding tube with a net of blood vessels around it, and arrows carrying small dots from the tube back into the vessels.

explanations.concept: Urine: what is in it, and where it goes
explanations.definition: Urine is the liquid left at the end of the nephrons. It is about 95 parts water in every 100, with urea, salts and other wastes dissolved in it.
explanations.description: Urine drips from the kidneys into the two ureters all day and all night. The ureters squeeze it down to the bladder. The bladder is a stretchy bag made of muscle. A nine-year-old's bladder holds about 300 millilitres, which is one and a half tumblers. When it is about half full, it signals the brain, and you feel the need to go. The yellow colour of urine has a long history. Old red blood cells are broken down in the liver. Bacteria in your gut then change the leftover colour. Part of it returns to the blood, and the kidneys send it out as a yellow waste called urobilin. Scientists found out how the bacteria do this only in 2024. When there is little water in your urine, the yellow is strong. When there is a lot of water, the yellow is pale.
examples: Pale yellow urine: plenty of water is leaving with the wastes.
Dark yellow urine: the kidneys are saving water, so the wastes are less thinned out.
Pink urine after beetroot: in some people, the beetroot's colour passes through the kidneys.
explanations.art: A side view of the two kidneys, two ureters and the bladder, with small yellow drops moving down the ureters.

explanations.concept: The kidneys change their work from hour to hour
explanations.definition: The kidneys keep the water and salt in the blood steady. They take back more at some times and less at others.
explanations.description: After you drink two tumblers of water, your blood becomes slightly more watery. Your brain notices this within minutes. It then makes less of a messenger chemical called ADH. With less ADH, the tubes of the nephrons take back less water. More water stays in the urine, so you pass more of it, and it is pale. On a hot day with little to drink, the opposite happens. The brain sends out more ADH, and the tubes take back almost all the water. You pass a little dark urine. The kidneys also slow down at night, which is why most children can sleep ten hours without a toilet visit. Salt is handled in the same way. After salty chips, the kidneys leave more salt in the urine.
examples: After a long drink: more urine, and paler.
After playing in the sun with no water: less urine, and darker.
At night: the kidneys make less urine than by day.
explanations.art: Two tumblers side by side, one nearly full of pale liquid and one with a little dark yellow liquid, each under a small drawing of the same child: one drinking, one playing in the sun.

explanations.concept: The lungs remove carbon dioxide, and other things too
explanations.definition: The lungs are a way out for wastes that can turn into a gas. Carbon dioxide passes from the blood into the air in the lungs and leaves in the breath.
explanations.description: Blood carries carbon dioxide from every cell to the lungs. There the blood flows very close to the air, with only a thin wall between them. Carbon dioxide passes through the wall, and you breathe it out. An adult breathes out about 1 kilogram of carbon dioxide a day. Breath also carries out water, about 300 millilitres a day. You see it as mist when you breathe on a cold steel tumbler. Other things in the blood can leave this way if they turn into a gas easily. After a person eats raw garlic, one of the garlic's smelly chemicals enters the blood from the gut. For hours it leaves through the lungs, however well the person brushes their teeth.
examples: Carbon dioxide: about 1 kilogram a day from an adult.
Water: the mist on a cold window when you breathe on it.
Garlic breath: a smell that comes from the blood, by way of the lungs.
explanations.art: A close view of a tiny air bag in a lung with a blood vessel around it, and small dots labelled CO2 crossing from the blood into the air.

explanations.concept: Sweat cools you, and carries a little waste
explanations.definition: Sweat is a liquid made by sweat glands in the skin. It is about 99 parts water in every 100, with salt and a very little urea.
explanations.description: A sweat gland is a tiny coiled tube deep in the skin. It draws water and salt from the liquid around it. The sweat rises through a duct to a pore on the skin. On the way up, the duct takes back much of the salt. This is the same method the kidney uses: let the liquid out first, then take back what is needed. On the skin, the water evaporates, which means it turns into a gas and goes into the air. Evaporating water carries heat away, and that is the main job of sweat. The salt cannot evaporate, so it stays on your skin and your clothes. Sweat does carry out a little urea. But the amount is tiny beside what the kidneys remove. A person cannot clean their blood by sweating.
examples: A white line on a dark cap after a hot cricket match: salt left by dried sweat.
A salty taste on your upper lip after running.
People who sweat often in hot places make less salty sweat, because their ducts take back more salt.
explanations.art: A cut through skin with a coiled sweat gland, a duct with arrows taking salt back, and drops on the surface turning into wavy lines of vapour.

explanations.concept: When kidneys stop working: dialysis and transplants
explanations.definition: Kidney failure means the kidneys can no longer clean the blood. Dialysis is cleaning the blood with a machine. A transplant is giving a person a healthy kidney from someone else.
explanations.description: When both kidneys fail, urea, salt and water build up in the blood. Without treatment a person dies within days or weeks. In 1943 the Dutch doctor Willem Kolff built the first artificial kidney that worked. He used sausage skin made of cellophane, a wooden drum and a tub of salty water. The patient's blood flowed through the cellophane tube. Cellophane has holes too small to see. Urea passed out through the holes into the tub, and the blood cells stayed in. Kolff's first patients died. In 1945 his machine saved Sofia Schafstadt, a woman of 67. Today's dialysis machines work on the same idea. A person can also live well with one kidney. So a healthy person can give one kidney to someone whose kidneys have failed. The first kidney transplant that lasted was done in 1954 in Boston, between twin brothers. The kidney that stays behind in the giver grows larger and does more work.
examples: Dialysis: about four hours on a machine, usually three times a week.
A transplant: one healthy kidney, often given by a parent, a sister or a brother.
Some people are born with one kidney and never notice.
explanations.art: A simple drawing of blood flowing through a thin tube lying in a tub of water, with small dots passing out through the tube's wall and large red discs staying inside.

explanations.concept: Why do we have two kidneys when one is enough?
explanations.description: A person with one healthy kidney can live a full life. So why does the body build two? Nobody is sure. Scientists have ideas, and each explains part of it.
examples: Eyes, ears, lungs and kidneys all come in pairs.
After one kidney is given away, the other grows and filters more.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study how bodies form
perspectives.explanation: A body grows as two matching halves, left and right. Many organs form once on each side, and the kidneys are among them. On this idea, two kidneys are a result of how a body is built.
A spare kidney helps an animal survive an injury, an illness or old age. Over a long life, each kidney slowly loses nephrons. On this idea, the second kidney is a reserve.

explanations.art: Two kidneys side by side, one drawn in full colour and one as a faint outline with a question mark.

agreed.text: The kidneys make urine by filtering the blood and then taking back most of what was filtered.
agreed.evidence: In 1924 Joseph Wearn and Alfred Newton Richards drew liquid from one glomerulus of a frog. They used a very fine glass pipette. It held salt and sugar but no protein. The frog's urine held no sugar.

agreed.text: An adult's kidneys filter about 180 litres a day and pass about 1 and a half litres as urine.
agreed.evidence: Doctors measure filtering with a harmless marker that passes the filter and is never taken back. The amount of marker in the urine shows how much liquid was filtered.

agreed.text: Carbon dioxide leaves the body through the lungs.
agreed.evidence: Breathed-out air holds about 100 times more carbon dioxide than breathed-in air. This has been measured since the time of Antoine Lavoisier in the 1780s.

agreed.text: Urea is made in the liver and removed by the kidneys.
agreed.evidence: When the kidneys fail, urea builds up in the blood, and dialysis brings it down. When the liver fails, ammonia builds up in the blood.

agreed.text: Sweat is mainly for cooling, and it removes only a small amount of waste.
agreed.evidence: Measurements of sweat show it is about 99 parts water in every 100. The urea in a day's sweat is a small fraction of the urea in a day's urine.

agreed.text: A person can live a healthy life with one kidney.
agreed.evidence: Doctors have followed thousands of people who gave a kidney, for many years. Most stay as healthy as other people of their age.

challenging.claim: You can sweat out toxins in a hot room or with hard exercise.
challenging.who: Many advertisements for saunas, hot yoga and 'detox' wraps.
challenging.for: Sweat does hold tiny traces of some pollutants, and people feel fresh after sweating.
challenging.against: In 2018 Pascal Imbeault and his team worked out the amounts. Even hard sweating removes far less of these pollutants than a day's food brings in. The liver and kidneys do the cleaning.

challenging.claim: Urine is sterile, which means it has no living microbes in it.
challenging.who: Doctors and textbooks for more than a hundred years.
challenging.for: The usual hospital test grew no bacteria from the urine of healthy people.
challenging.against: In 2014 Evann Hilt, Alan Wolfe, Linda Brubaker and their team used better ways to grow bacteria. They found living bacteria in the bladders of healthy women. The bladder has its own community of microbes.

challenging.claim: Everyone must drink eight glasses of water a day.
challenging.who: Health magazines, apps and many school posters.
challenging.for: The body does lose water all day, and too little water makes the kidneys' work harder.
challenging.against: In 2002 the kidney scientist Heinz Valtin searched for the evidence behind the number and found none. Food also gives water. Needs differ with size, weather and play. Thirst and urine colour are better guides.

challenging.claim: Drinking your own urine is good for your health.
challenging.who: Some old health traditions. Morarji Desai, a prime minister of India, said in public that he did it.
challenging.for: People who do it say they feel well, and urine from a healthy person is mostly water.
challenging.against: No fair test has shown any benefit. Urine holds the very wastes that the kidneys worked to remove. Drinking it gives them back to the kidneys to remove again.

challenging.claim: The salt in our blood is left over from the ancient sea where animals first lived.
challenging.who: The Canadian scientist Archibald Macallum, in 1926.
challenging.for: Blood is salty, and the first animals did live in the sea. The mix of salts in blood is a little like sea water.
challenging.against: Blood is about three times less salty than today's sea. Nobody knows exactly how salty the ancient sea was. The idea is attractive, but it is hard to test.

big_questions.q: Your kidneys can remove a new medicine that no human body ever met before. Could a cleaner that only hunts for known dirt do that?
big_questions.hint: Think about the Three Filters Test. The kidneys only need to know what to take back.

big_questions.q: Urea is a waste to you and a food to a plant. Is anything a waste for everyone?
big_questions.hint: Farmers put urea on fields. Bacteria in the soil turn the urea into a form that roots take in.

big_questions.q: Food that you could not digest passes through your gut and never enters a cell. Was it ever inside you?
big_questions.hint: The gut is a tube that runs through the body, open at both ends.

big_questions.q: About half the water in your body is replaced every week or two. Are you the same body you were last year?
big_questions.hint: The water changes, but the pattern of your body stays. Which one is you?

big_questions.q: There are more people who need a kidney than there are kidneys given. How should we decide who gets one?
big_questions.hint: Some say the person who has waited longest. Some say the person the kidney fits best. Some say children first.

big_questions.q: Astronauts drink water that was cleaned from their own urine. Is that different from what the Earth does with all water?
big_questions.hint: The water in your tumbler has passed through many animals, including humans, plants and clouds before.

story.title: What Fell Through the Sieve
story.note: Yazhini, Selvi Chithi, Kathir and the stall are made up. It is true that many tailors work in small stalls in the lanes around the Meenakshi temple in Madurai. The way Yazhini cleans the heap is the way a kidney cleans blood. A filter holds back the big things, everything small passes through, and only what is needed is taken back.
text: The day before the wedding order was due, the button tin fell off the top shelf.

Yazhini heard it from the back of the stall. First there was a bang, and then a sound like heavy rain on a tin roof. Then came the small voice of her cousin Kathir, who was five. "I only wanted to see the bells," he said.

Her aunt's tailoring stall stood in a lane near the Meenakshi temple in Madurai. On one side sat a bangle seller. On the other was a shop that sold sieves, winnowing trays and brass pots. The stall was four steps wide, and every wall was shelves.

The tin was an old biscuit tin as big as a pillow. Selvi Chithi had been filling it for twenty years. It held shell buttons and brass buttons, hooks and eyes, press studs, sequins and glass beads. It held the tiny silver bells that are sewn on the hem of a little girl's pavadai.

Now all of it lay on the floor. And the floor of a tailoring stall is never empty. There were thread ends and snips of cloth, chalk dust and pins. There were three spools that had rolled under the machine, pieces of a broken bangle from next door, and the sand that comes in on everybody's feet.

Chithi looked at the heap. Then she looked at the clock. "Forty shell buttons and sixty silver hooks for the wedding blouses," she said. "They are wanted by six. And I have nine hems still to do." She sat down at her machine. "Yazhi, you clean it. Take out the rubbish and put the rest back in the tin."

Yazhini knelt on the floor and began. She picked out a thread end. Then she picked out a snip of blue cloth, and a piece of bangle glass, carefully, by its smooth side. Then a burnt matchstick. Then something grey and soft that she did not want to name.
After half an hour she had filled a paper cone with rubbish, and the heap looked exactly the same.

Every handful held a new kind of rubbish. There was a toffee wrapper, a curl of pencil shaving and a dry neem leaf. There was a fish scale, and nobody could say how a fish scale had come to a tailor's stall. Some things she could not name at all. How do you pick out a thing when you do not know what it is?
And then there was the sand. No fingers can pick out sand.
"I can blow on it," said Kathir. He blew. Sand flew up, and forty sequins flew with it and went under the shelves.
"Thank you, Kathir," said Yazhini. "Please do not help."

She sat back on her heels. Her knees hurt. The clock said a quarter past three. At her machine, Chithi dropped a needle. Chithi did not look at the dust or the threads on the floor. She looked for one bright thing, found it, picked it up and went on sewing. It took her two seconds.
Yazhini watched that, and then she looked at her paper cone.

The rubbish had no end of kinds. She would never learn them all. But the things the stall wanted were few, and she knew every one of them. Buttons. Hooks and eyes. Press studs. Sequins. Beads. Bells. She could count them on six fingers.
She stood up and went next door. "Akka, may I borrow a sieve for one hour? The one with the big holes, for cleaning groundnuts."
Back in the stall she spread a clean white veshti on the floor. She held the sieve over it and shook the whole heap through, a few handfuls at a time.

The big things stayed in the sieve. There were the three spools, the measuring tape and some pieces of cloth large enough to use as patches. They were easy to see, and nearly all of them belonged to the stall. She put them back on the shelf.
Everything small had fallen through. It lay on the white cloth in a thin layer, the buttons and the sand together, the bells and the dust and the fish scale.

Now Yazhini did not look for rubbish at all. She set out six steel tumblers. She looked only for the six kinds of things, and her fingers found them quickly. A button feels like a button. A hook catches on the skin. She gave Kathir the tumbler for bells, because bells shine and ring, and even a boy of five can find them.
"Fifty-one bells!" said Kathir, much later, and nobody checked.

When the tumblers were full, Yazhini looked at what was left on the veshti. Sand. Dust. Thread. Glass. The grey soft thing. Things with names and things without names. She did not sort them. She did not need to know a single one of them. She gathered the four corners of the cloth, carried it to the bin at the end of the lane and shook it out.
At five o'clock she counted forty shell buttons and sixty silver hooks into two paper packets and put them beside the machine.
Chithi stopped the wheel with her hand. "Finished? I thought you would still be picking out threads at Pongal."
"I stopped picking out the rubbish," said Yazhini. "I let everything small fall through. Then I took back what we wanted. The rest left by itself."
Chithi turned a shell button over in her fingers. "So if a new kind of rubbish falls on my floor tomorrow?"
"Then it goes out with the sand," said Yazhini. "I never have to know what it is."
Chithi laughed, bit off her thread and reached for the first blouse. Kathir sat under the shelves and looked for sequins, one bright thing at a time.
story.epiphany: Yazhini could not finish while she tried to pick out the rubbish, because rubbish comes in endless kinds. She finished when she let everything small fall through the sieve and took back only what the stall needed. Your kidneys clean your blood in the same way.
ask: Why did picking out the rubbish take so long, while picking out the buttons was quick?
What stayed in the sieve, and what fell through? Which things in your blood are like each of these?
A new kind of rubbish falls on the floor the next day. Why does Yazhini's method still work?
