games.title: Stopped, Back or Out? The kidney sorting game
games.context: This is a card game about what happens inside a kidney. Each card names something in the blood. You say whether the kidney stops it, takes it back or sends it out.

setup.art: Twenty-four cards in a shuffled pile on a table, with three small tokens marked STOPPED, BACK and OUT in front of each of two players.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the 24 cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile.

setup.art: One child reading a card aloud while another player slides one token forward, face down.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads the front. Everyone else puts down one token, face down.

setup.art: The tokens turned face up and the reader showing the back of the card.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the tokens over. The reader reads the back.

printables.title: 24 kidney cards: something in the blood on the front, what the kidney does with it on the back

items.f: A red blood cell.
items.b: STOPPED. A red blood cell is far too big for the holes in the filter. It stays in the blood.

items.f: A white blood cell, which fights germs.
items.b: STOPPED. A white blood cell is even bigger than a red one. It stays in the blood.

items.f: A platelet, a tiny piece of a cell that helps blood to clot.
items.b: STOPPED. A platelet is small for a cell part, but still too big for the filter.

items.f: A large protein that carries things around in the blood.
items.b: STOPPED. Large proteins are too big to pass. Protein in the urine is a sign that the filters are hurt.

items.f: An antibody, a large protein that sticks to germs.
items.b: STOPPED. An antibody is a large protein. It stays in the blood to do its work.

items.f: Sugar, on an ordinary day.
items.b: BACK. Sugar passes the filter. Then the tube takes all of it back, because cells need sugar for energy.

items.f: Sugar, just after you have eaten a ripe banana.
items.b: BACK. A healthy kidney still takes all the sugar back, even after a sweet snack.

items.f: An amino acid, a building block of protein.
items.b: BACK. Amino acids pass the filter. The tube takes them back, because the body builds with them.

items.f: Water. You have played in the sun for two hours and drunk nothing.
items.b: BACK. Your body is short of water. The tube takes back nearly all of it, and your urine is dark.

items.f: Water. It is night, and you are fast asleep.
items.b: BACK. At night the kidneys take back more water and make less urine. That is why you can sleep through.

items.f: Salt. You have sweated a lot and eaten very little salt today.
items.b: BACK. Your body is short of salt. The tube takes back nearly all of it.

items.f: Calcium. You are nine and your bones are growing.
items.b: BACK. Calcium passes the filter. The tube takes back nearly all of it for your bones.

items.f: Water, on an ordinary day.
items.b: BACK. On an ordinary day about 99 of every 100 parts of the water return to the blood.

items.f: Urea, the waste from using protein.
items.b: OUT. Urea passes the filter, and much of it stays in the tube. It leaves in the urine.

items.f: Creatinine, a waste made by working muscles.
items.b: OUT. Creatinine passes the filter, and the tube does not take it back. All of it leaves.

items.f: Water. You have just drunk three tumblers in a row.
items.b: OUT. Your blood has more water than it needs. The tube takes back less, and you pass a lot of pale urine.

items.f: Salt. You have just eaten a whole packet of salty chips.
items.b: OUT. Your blood has more salt than it needs. The tube leaves the extra salt in the urine.

items.f: Potassium. You have just drunk two tender coconuts.
items.b: OUT. Tender coconut water is rich in potassium. The tube sends the extra out.

items.f: Vitamin C. You have just eaten four amla, far more than you need.
items.b: OUT. The body cannot store much vitamin C. The extra passes into the urine.

items.f: What is left of a fever medicine, after it has done its work.
items.b: OUT. Nothing in the tube takes it back. So it leaves, though your body never met it before.

items.f: Urobilin, the yellow colour made from old red blood cells.
items.b: OUT. Urobilin stays in the tube. It is what makes urine yellow.

items.f: Acid, made when the body uses protein.
items.b: OUT. The tube pushes extra acid into the urine. This keeps the blood from becoming too acid.

items.f: The red colour of beetroot, in a person whose gut lets it into the blood.
items.b: OUT. In some people the colour reaches the blood. It passes the filter, stays in the tube and turns the urine pink.

items.f: Sugar, in a person whose blood holds far too much of it.
items.b: OUT, in part. The tube takes back all it can, but some sugar is left over. Doctors test urine for sugar to find diabetes.

printables.title: 3 tokens: STOPPED, BACK, OUT. Print one set for each player
items: STOPPED: too big for the filter, so it stays in the blood
BACK: passes the filter, then the tube takes it back
OUT: passes the filter, stays in the tube and leaves in the urine

rules: One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader keeps the back hidden.
Every other player chooses one token and puts it face down. STOPPED means it is too big for the filter. BACK means the tube takes it back. OUT means it leaves in the urine.
Everyone turns the tokens over together. The reader reads the back of the card.
Every player whose token matches the back scores 1 point. A player who also gives the reason, before the back is read, scores 1 more.
With two players, swap the reader's role after every card. The reader does not guess on their own card.
Playing alone? Read a card, say STOPPED, BACK or OUT aloud, then turn the card over. Score 1 point for each right answer.
After all 24 cards, the player with the most points wins. If you play alone, your score out of 24 is your result.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile. Give each player one set of three tokens.
flow.say: Each card names something that is in the blood as it reaches a kidney. First ask if it is small enough to pass the filter. If it passes, ask if the body needs it back.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Take three tokens.
flow.context: This is the first step of Stopped, Back or Out. You set up the cards and the tokens.

flow.do: Play the first twelve cards. After each card, read the back aloud. Ask the question below after card six.
flow.say: The reader reads the front. Choose a token and put it face down. Now turn it over. The reader reads the back. Who scored?
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Pick a token. Turn it over. Check the back.

ask.q: How did you decide between BACK and OUT?
good: I asked if the body needs it.
I looked at what the person had just done, such as drinking a lot.
Wastes like urea go out.

flow.parent: A useful question for a stuck child is: is it a whole cell or a large protein? If so, it is stopped. One child can play alone or with you.
flow.context: In this step of Stopped, Back or Out you play the first twelve kidney cards.

flow.do: Play the last twelve cards the same way. Keep the score on a piece of paper.
flow.say: Twelve more cards. Notice the cards for water and for salt. The answer changes with what the person has been doing.
flow.kid: Play twelve more cards. Watch the water and salt cards closely.
flow.context: In this step of Stopped, Back or Out you play the last twelve kidney cards. You watch how the answer changes for water and salt.

flow.do: Count the points. Then sort all 24 cards into three piles by their backs and look at the piles.
flow.say: Let us sort the cards into three piles. Look at the OUT pile. Did the kidney have to recognise each of these as a waste?
flow.kid: Sort the cards into three piles. What is in the OUT pile?

check.q: Water is in the BACK pile and also in the OUT pile. Why?
options: The kidney takes back what the body needs
The kidney treats water at random
Some water is too big for the filter
check.why: The tube takes back more water when the body is short of it, and less after a long drink. All water passes the filter, because water particles are very small.

flow.context: This is the last step of Stopped, Back or Out. You sort the kidney cards into three piles and compare them.

games.title: Which Way Out? A running game with four exits
games.context: This is a running game about the ways things leave the body. A caller reads a card, and the players run to the sign for the right way out.

setup.art: Four paper signs marked LUNGS, KIDNEYS, SKIN and GUT stuck in four corners of a room.
setup.caption: 1. Put the four signs in four corners of a room.

setup.art: A grown-up reading from a card while two children stand in the middle of the room, ready to run.
setup.caption: 2. The caller reads the front of a card. The players run to a sign.

setup.art: A child standing by the LUNGS sign while the caller shows the back of the card.
setup.caption: 3. The caller reads the back. A player at a right sign scores 1 point.

printables.title: 4 exit signs
items: LUNGS: things leave as gas in the breath
KIDNEYS: things leave dissolved in urine
GUT: things leave in the stool

printables.title: 16 call cards: something that leaves the body on the front, its way out on the back

items.f: Carbon dioxide made by your leg muscles as you run.
items.b: LUNGS. Blood carries it to the lungs, and you breathe it out.

items.f: Urea made by your liver after a bowl of sambar.
items.b: KIDNEYS. Urea dissolves in the blood, and the kidneys send it out in urine.

items.f: The skins of sweetcorn that you could not digest.
items.b: GUT. They passed through the gut and never entered your blood.

items.f: The salt in the white line on a cap after a hot match.
items.b: SKIN. Sweat dried on the cap. The water went into the air and the salt stayed.

items.f: The extra water from three tumblers of buttermilk.
items.b: KIDNEYS. The kidneys take back less water, and you pass more urine.

items.f: The mist on a cold steel tumbler when you breathe on it.
items.b: LUNGS. Your breath carries out water as a gas. It turns to drops on the cold steel.

items.f: The smell of raw garlic, two hours after lunch.
items.b: LUNGS. A garlic chemical enters the blood and leaves through the lungs for hours.

items.f: The yellow colour in urine.
items.b: KIDNEYS. It is urobilin, made from old red blood cells.

items.f: The brown colour in a stool.
items.b: GUT. The liver makes it from old red blood cells and sends it into the gut.

items.f: The extra salt from a packet of salty mixture.
items.b: KIDNEYS. The kidneys leave the extra salt in the urine. SKIN also scores if you are sweating.

items.f: What is left of a cough medicine, a day after you took it.
items.b: KIDNEYS. Most used medicines leave dissolved in the urine.

items.f: The water in the wet patch on your shirt after football.
items.b: SKIN. It is sweat. It cools you as it dries.

items.f: Dead bacteria from your large intestine.
items.b: GUT. A large part of every stool is gut bacteria.

items.f: Creatinine, a waste from working muscles.
items.b: KIDNEYS. It passes the filter and is never taken back.

items.f: Carbon dioxide made by your brain cells while you sleep.
items.b: LUNGS. Your cells make carbon dioxide all night, and your lungs remove it all night.

items.f: The seeds of a guava that you swallowed whole.
items.b: GUT. The seeds pass through the gut unchanged.

rules: Stick the four signs in four corners of a room. All players stand in the middle.
One person is the caller. The caller reads the front of the top card aloud.
The players run to the sign they choose. Each player must touch the wall under a sign before the caller counts to five.
The caller reads the back. Each player at a sign named on the back scores 1 point.
Everyone returns to the middle, and the caller reads the next card.
Playing alone or with one parent? The parent calls, and the child runs. Or lay the signs on a table and place each card on a sign.
After all 16 cards, the player with the most points wins. Alone, try to beat your own score next time.

flow.do: Stick the four signs in four corners of a room. Shuffle the 16 cards. Clear the floor so that nobody trips.
flow.say: There are four ways out of the body in this game. I will read out something that leaves the body. Run to the way out you think it takes.
flow.kid: Put up the four signs. Stand in the middle of the room.
flow.context: This is the first step of Which Way Out. You put up the four exit signs.

flow.do: Read the 16 cards one at a time. After each run, read the back aloud and give the points.
flow.say: Listen to the whole card before you run. Ask yourself: is it a gas, is it dissolved in the blood, or was it never in the blood?
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Run to a sign. Hear the answer.
flow.parent: In a small flat, players can point or hop instead of running. With one child, you are the caller.
flow.context: In this step of Which Way Out you hear 16 cards. For each one you run to the lungs, kidneys, skin or gut sign.

flow.do: Count the points. Lay the cards under the four signs and look at the GUT pile together.
flow.say: Look at the cards under GUT. Three of them were never inside the blood at all. Which ones? And which one was made by the body?
flow.kid: Count your points. Look at the gut cards. Which were never in your blood?

check.q: Which of these was made by your own cells?
options: The carbon dioxide in your breath
check.why: Your cells make carbon dioxide when they use food for energy. Guava seeds and sweetcorn skins are food that was never digested. They passed through the gut without entering a cell.

flow.context: This is the last step of Which Way Out. You compare the cards under the gut sign with the other three piles.

experiments.title: The Three Filters Test: what can a filter hold back?
experiments.question: A mixture holds tea leaves, flour, tea colour and salt. Which of these four can a tea strainer hold back? Which can a cloth hold back? Which can tissue paper hold back?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which of the four things will the tissue paper hold back: the tea leaves, the flour, the tea colour, the salt? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use one mixture for all three filters, and stir it just before each pour. Pour the same amount through each filter, about a third of the tumbler. Use the same tea strainer each time, and rinse it between pours. Check every bowl in the same four ways. Only one thing changes: the size of the holes in the filter.
results_table: Can you see the spoon at the bottom?

materials.item: drinking water, one tumbler (200 millilitres), heated by a grown-up until hot
tea leaves or tea dust, 1 teaspoon
salt, 1 level teaspoon
atta or rice flour, 1 level teaspoon
a steel tea strainer
a clean, thin cotton cloth, such as a handkerchief, about 20 centimetres wide
paper tissues or paper napkins (two layers of toilet paper also work)
small steel bowls (katoris), all the same size
steel teaspoons
a steel tumbler for the mixture, and a notebook page for the results

experiments.safety: A grown-up heats and pours the hot water. Let the mixture cool until it is just warm before the child handles it. Use drinking water and clean things, because the child tastes one drop from each bowl.
experiments.record: Draw a table with three rows: strainer, cloth and tissue. For each row write yes or no four times: tea leaves, spoon seen, brown colour, salty taste.
experiments.context: In this experiment you make a mixture of tea, salt and flour. You pour it through a tea strainer, a cloth and a paper tissue, and check what each filter holds back.

setup.art: A steel tumbler of brown tea with tea leaves at the bottom, and a child stirring in a teaspoon of salt and a teaspoon of flour.
setup.caption: 1. Make tea in a tumbler. Stir in 1 teaspoon of salt and 1 teaspoon of flour.

setup.art: A tea strainer held over a small steel bowl, with cloudy brown liquid pouring through it and tea leaves collecting in the strainer.
setup.caption: 2. Pour a third of the mixture through the strainer into the first bowl.

setup.art: The same strainer lined with a thin cotton cloth over a second bowl, and beside it the strainer lined with a paper tissue over a third bowl.
setup.caption: 3. Line the strainer with cloth for the second bowl, and with tissue for the third.

setup.art: A child lowering a steel teaspoon to the bottom of a bowl of liquid and looking down at it.
setup.caption: 4. The spoon check: lower a spoon to the bottom. Can you still see it?

setup.art: A notebook table with three rows labelled strainer, cloth and tissue, and yes or no written in four columns.
setup.caption: 5. Check each bowl for leaves, cloudiness, colour and salty taste. Write yes or no.

flow.do: Put 1 teaspoon of tea leaves in a steel tumbler. A grown-up pours in one tumbler of hot water. Wait 5 minutes. Then stir in 1 level teaspoon of salt until it is gone.
flow.say: This is our mixture. The tea has turned the water brown. Now the salt goes in. Stir, and tell me where the salt has gone.
flow.kid: Watch the tea turn brown. Stir in the salt. Where did the salt go?
flow.parent: While the tea stands, read the question together. The salt has dissolved. It is still there, as particles too small to see.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Three Filters Test. You make tea in a tumbler and dissolve salt in it.

flow.do: Let the tea cool until it is just warm. Stir in 1 level teaspoon of atta. Then ask for the guess and the reason for each of the four things. Write them down.
flow.say: The mixture now holds four things: tea leaves, flour, brown colour and salt. We will pour it through three filters. Which of the four will the tissue hold back? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Stir in the flour. Guess what the tissue will hold back. Say why.

ask.q: Why do you think the tissue will hold that back?
good: The leaves are big.
The tissue has very small holes.
A filter cleans water, so it takes out the salt.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children expect the tissue to take out the salt or the colour. The test will answer it.
flow.context: In this step of the Three Filters Test you add flour to the salty tea. Then you guess what each filter will hold back.

flow.do: Stir the mixture well. At once pour about a third of it through the bare tea strainer into bowl 1. Rinse the strainer.
flow.say: First filter: the strainer alone. Stir, then pour quickly, before the leaves sink. What stayed in the strainer?
flow.kid: Stir. Pour a third through the strainer into bowl 1.
flow.context: In this step of the Three Filters Test you pour salty tea with flour in it through a bare tea strainer.

flow.do: Line the strainer with one layer of cotton cloth. Stir the mixture and pour half of what is left into bowl 2. Then line the strainer with two tissues. Stir, and pour the rest slowly into bowl 3.
flow.say: Second filter: the cloth. Third filter: the tissue. The tissue is slow, so pour a little at a time. Do not squeeze it.
flow.kid: Pour through the cloth into bowl 2. Pour through the tissue into bowl 3.
flow.parent: The tissue may take 3 to 5 minutes and may clog. If it is still dripping after 5 minutes, lift it away. A few spoonfuls in bowl 3 are enough. A squeezed tissue tears, and the test is spoilt.
flow.context: In this step of the Three Filters Test you pour salty tea with flour in it through a cloth. Then you pour it through a paper tissue.

flow.do: Check each bowl in four ways. Look for leaves. Lower a clean spoon to the bottom and see if it shows. Look at the colour. Taste one drop from a clean spoon. Write yes or no in the table.
flow.say: Now we check each bowl. Are there leaves? Can you see the spoon at the bottom? Is it brown? Is one drop salty? Use a fresh spoon for each taste.
flow.kid: Check each bowl. Leaves? Spoon seen? Brown? Salty? Write yes or no.

check.q: In the Three Filters Test, why do you stir the mixture before every pour?
options: So each filter gets the same mixture
check.why: Leaves and flour sink. Without stirring, the last pour would get most of them, and the test would not be fair. If you chose 'the salt becomes bigger', remember that stirring does not change the size of a dissolved particle.

flow.parent: In most homes the strainer stops the leaves and the cloth stops some flour. The tissue stops nearly all the flour. All three bowls are brown and salty. Bowl 3 may still be slightly hazy. Write what you really see.
flow.context: In this step of the Three Filters Test you check three bowls of filtered tea. You look for leaves, cloudiness, colour and salt.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. After they have answered, read them the note below.
flow.say: Look at your table. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Which things did no filter hold back?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why.

ask.q: Why did the salt pass through every filter?
good: It dissolved into particles smaller than the holes.
It is far too small to be caught.

ask.q: Your blood holds useful salt and sugar. What happens to them at a filter in your kidney?
good: They pass through with the water.
The kidney must get them back somehow.

flow.parent: The reason: a filter sorts only by size. Leaves are bigger than the strainer's holes. Flour grains are bigger than the tissue's holes. Dissolved salt and tea colour are single particles, thousands of times smaller than any hole in a tissue. The filters in a kidney have much finer holes. They hold back blood cells and large proteins. But salt, sugar and urea pass through together. So filtering alone cannot clean blood. The kidney needs a second step, which is to take back the salt, the sugar and most of the water.
flow.think: If no filter can separate salt from water, how might the kidney get its salt back?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Three Filters Test. You say what the strainer, the cloth and the tissue held back from the salty tea.

experiments.title: After Two Tumblers: how soon do your kidneys answer?
experiments.question: You drink two tumblers of water at 3 o'clock. How long is it until the extra water leaves as urine? How do the colour and the amount of urine change, compared with an ordinary afternoon?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. How many minutes after the two tumblers will you first need the toilet? Will the urine be paler, darker or the same as usual? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Do both afternoons at home, with the same kind of lunch and the same kind of quiet play. On both days, use the toilet at 3 o'clock, and then record every visit until 6 o'clock. On the ordinary day, drink only a few sips if you are thirsty. On the water day, drink two tumblers at 3 o'clock. Only one thing changes: the two tumblers of water.
results_table: How long the stream lasted, in counts

materials.item: drinking water, two tumblers (400 millilitres)
a clock
a notebook page and a pencil, kept near the toilet
yellow and orange colour pencils or crayons, for the colour chart

schedule.what: The ordinary afternoon. Draw the colour chart. Record every toilet visit from 3 o'clock to 6 o'clock.
The water afternoon. Drink two tumblers at 3 o'clock. Record every visit until 6 o'clock, then compare the two days.

experiments.record: A colour chart with four boxes: 1 nearly clear, 2 pale yellow, 3 yellow, 4 dark yellow. A table for each day with the time, the colour shade and the count for every toilet visit.
experiments.context: In this two-day experiment you record your toilet visits on an ordinary afternoon. The next afternoon you drink two tumblers of water at 3 o'clock and record the visits again.

setup.art: A notebook page with four small boxes coloured from nearly clear to dark yellow and numbered 1 to 4.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a colour chart with four shades of yellow, numbered 1 to 4.

setup.art: A child drinking from a steel tumbler beside a wall clock that shows 3 o'clock, with a second full tumbler waiting.
setup.caption: 2. On the water day, drink two tumblers at 3 o'clock.

setup.art: A notebook table with rows of times, shade numbers and counts, hanging on a hook beside a bathroom door.
setup.caption: 3. After every toilet visit, write the time, the shade and your count.

flow.do: Day 1. Draw the colour chart with your child: four boxes from nearly clear to dark yellow. Ask for the guess about tomorrow, and the reason. Write both down.
flow.say: Tomorrow at 3 o'clock you will drink two tumblers of water. How many minutes later will you first need the toilet? Will the urine look different? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Draw four shades of yellow. Guess how soon the water comes out. Say why.

ask.q: Why do you think it will take that long?
good: The water has to go from the stomach into the blood first.
The kidneys need time to notice.
It goes straight through, so it will be quick.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children think water runs straight from the stomach to the bladder.
flow.context: This is the first step of After Two Tumblers. You draw a colour chart for urine and guess what two tumblers of water will do.

flow.do: Day 1. At 3 o'clock your child uses the toilet. This visit is not recorded. Until 6 o'clock they record every visit: the time, the shade, and how long the stream lasted, counted slowly.
flow.say: This is the ordinary afternoon. Use the toilet now, to start with an empty bladder. After each visit until 6 o'clock, write the time, the shade and your count.
flow.kid: Use the toilet at 3 o'clock. After that, write down every visit.
flow.parent: Counting 'one, two, three' during the stream is a simple measure of the amount. There may be no visit at all in three hours. Write that down. It is a result.
flow.context: In this step of After Two Tumblers you record your toilet visits on an ordinary afternoon. You record from 3 o'clock to 6 o'clock.

flow.do: Day 2. Give the same kind of lunch. At 3 o'clock your child uses the toilet, then drinks two tumblers of water within 10 minutes. Until 6 o'clock they record every visit as before.
flow.say: This is the water afternoon. Use the toilet, then drink both tumblers. Now watch the clock. Tell me the moment you first need to go.
flow.kid: Use the toilet. Drink two tumblers. Write down every visit until 6 o'clock.
flow.wait: Do this the day after the ordinary afternoon
flow.parent: Two tumblers are a safe amount for a child of nine. Do not give more. Most children first need the toilet 30 to 60 minutes after drinking, and go two or three times.
flow.context: In this step of After Two Tumblers you drink two tumblers of water at 3 o'clock. Then you record every toilet visit until 6 o'clock.

flow.do: Day 2, after 6 o'clock. Put the two tables side by side. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. Then read them the note below.
flow.say: Look at both days. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. How many minutes passed before the first visit on the water day?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why.

ask.q: The water did not come out at once. Where was it during that time?
good: In the stomach and gut, then in the blood.
The kidneys had to filter it out of the blood.

ask.q: Why was the urine paler on the water day?
good: More water left with the same wastes.
The yellow was thinned out.

check.q: After two tumblers of water, why does urine become paler?
options: The same wastes leave in more water
check.why: The kidneys go on removing the same wastes. They take back less water, so the yellow colour is spread through more liquid. If you chose 'the kidneys stop removing wastes', remember that cells never stop making waste.

flow.parent: The reason: water goes from the gut into the blood in a few minutes. The brain senses that the blood is more watery and sends less of the messenger ADH. The tubes in the kidneys then take back less water. The extra water reaches the bladder within about half an hour to an hour. If your child was short of water before the test, less comes out. The body kept what it needed. Vitamin tablets can turn urine bright yellow, and beetroot can turn it pink.
flow.context: This is the last step of After Two Tumblers. You compare your toilet visits on the ordinary afternoon and on the water afternoon.

activities.title: Find Your Kidneys: two thumbs on your back

materials.item: a sheet of paper and a pencil
a yellow colour pencil or crayon

schedule.what: Find your kidneys with your thumbs and draw the path of urine.

activities.record: A drawing of a body outline with two kidneys, two ureters and a bladder. A yellow line runs from each kidney to the bladder.
activities.context: In this activity you find where your two kidneys are, using your thumbs. Then you draw the path that urine takes from the kidneys to the bladder.

setup.art: A child seen from behind, hands on her waist, thumbs pressed on her back just under her lowest ribs.
setup.caption: 1. Hands on your waist, thumbs on your back. Slide up to your lowest ribs.

setup.art: A child holding her fist beside her lower back.
setup.caption: 2. Make a fist. Each kidney is about this size.

setup.art: A pencil drawing of a body outline with two bean shapes in the back, two thin tubes and a round bag low in the belly.
setup.caption: 3. Draw the two kidneys, the two ureters and the bladder.

flow.do: Ask your child to point to where they think their kidneys are. Ask how big they think one kidney is. Do not correct them yet.
flow.say: You have two kidneys. Point to where you think they are. Show me with your hands how big you think one is.
flow.kid: Point to where your kidneys are. Show how big one is.
flow.parent: Many children point low in the belly, where the bladder is.
flow.context: This is the first step of Find Your Kidneys. You guess where your kidneys are and how big they are.

flow.do: Your child puts both hands on their waist, thumbs on the back. They slide their hands up until the thumbs touch the lowest ribs. Then they make a fist and hold it there.
flow.say: Hands on your waist, thumbs behind. Slide up until your thumbs meet your lowest ribs. Your kidneys are under your thumbs, one each side of your backbone. Each is about the size of your fist.
flow.kid: Thumbs on your back, under your lowest ribs. Your kidneys are there.

options: In my back, just under my lowest ribs
Low in my belly, at the front
In my chest, beside my heart
check.why: The kidneys lie at the back, one on each side of the backbone, partly covered by the lowest ribs. Low in the belly at the front is the bladder, which only stores the urine.

flow.context: In this step of Find Your Kidneys you find your kidneys with your thumbs. They are in your back, just under your lowest ribs.

flow.do: Your child draws a body outline. They add two kidneys, a ureter from each one and the bladder. They colour the path of urine yellow.
flow.say: Draw the two kidneys high in the back. Draw a thin tube from each one down to the bladder. Now trace a sip of water from your mouth to your bladder.
flow.kid: Draw two kidneys, two tubes and a bladder. Colour the path yellow.

ask.q: Which way does a sip of water travel to reach your bladder?
good: Mouth, stomach and gut, then into the blood.
The blood carries it to the kidneys.
From the kidneys down the ureters to the bladder.

flow.parent: There is no tube from the stomach to the bladder. All water reaches the kidneys through the blood.
flow.context: This is the last step of Find Your Kidneys. You draw the kidneys, the ureters and the bladder, and trace the path of water through the body.

activities.title: Ninety-Nine Back: one litre and two teaspoons

materials.item: a one-litre bottle, filled with water
a teaspoon
a steel tumbler
a bathroom bucket

schedule.what: Measure out how much of one litre of filtered liquid becomes urine.

activities.record: Write three numbers. The first is your guess for the urine an adult passes in a day. The second is the real amount. The third is the teaspoons of urine that come from one litre of filtered liquid.
activities.context: In this activity you use a litre bottle and a teaspoon. You see how much of the liquid filtered by the kidneys goes back into the blood.

setup.art: A full one-litre bottle of water on a table beside a teaspoon, an empty steel tumbler and a bucket.
setup.caption: 1. Fill a one-litre bottle. This stands for one litre of liquid filtered out of the blood.

setup.art: A child pouring one teaspoon of water from the bottle into the tumbler.
setup.caption: 2. Take out 2 teaspoons. This small amount becomes urine.

setup.art: The bottle, still almost full, with an arrow pointing back towards a drawing of a blood vessel.
setup.caption: 3. All the rest goes back into the blood.

flow.do: Show the bucket and find out how many litres it holds. Tell your child that an adult's kidneys filter 180 litres a day. Ask them to guess how much urine an adult passes in a day.
flow.say: An adult's kidneys filter about 180 litres of liquid out of the blood each day. That is many buckets. How much urine do you think an adult passes in a day? Why?
flow.kid: Kidneys filter 180 litres a day. Guess how much becomes urine.
flow.parent: Most bathroom buckets hold 15 to 20 litres. With a 15-litre bucket, 180 litres is 12 buckets. An adult has only about 5 litres of blood.
flow.context: This is the first step of Ninety-Nine Back. You guess how much of the 180 litres filtered by an adult's kidneys becomes urine.

flow.do: Give the answer: about 1 and a half litres. Fill the one-litre bottle. Your child takes out 2 teaspoons of water and puts them in the tumbler.
flow.say: An adult passes about 1 and a half litres of urine a day. So from each litre filtered, only about 2 teaspoons become urine. Take out 2 teaspoons. Look at what is left in the bottle.
flow.kid: Take 2 teaspoons from the litre. That much becomes urine.
flow.parent: Two teaspoons are 10 millilitres, which is 1 part in 100 of a litre. The true share is a little under that.
flow.context: In this step of Ninety-Nine Back you take 2 teaspoons from a litre of water. This shows how little of the filtered liquid becomes urine.

flow.do: Hold up the bottle and the tumbler. Talk about the questions below.
flow.say: The bottle goes back into the blood. The tumbler leaves the body. Why would the kidneys filter so much, only to take nearly all of it back?
flow.kid: The bottle goes back to the blood. Why filter so much?

ask.q: Why filter so much and take almost all of it back?
good: Every small waste gets pushed out, even ones the body does not know.
The blood gets cleaned again and again.
The kidney only has to choose what to keep.

check.q: Of every 100 parts of liquid that the kidneys filter, about how many go back into the blood?
check.why: About 99 parts go back and about 1 part leaves as urine. If you chose 1, you may have swapped the two numbers.

flow.parent: The 180 litres are filtered out of only about 3 litres of the watery part of an adult's blood. So that liquid is cleaned about 60 times a day.
flow.context: This is the last step of Ninety-Nine Back. You ask why the kidneys filter 180 litres a day and take back about 99 parts in every 100.

activities.title: The Garlic Breath Test: can brushing remove a smell from the blood?

materials.item: a small clove of raw garlic, peeled and chopped
a spoon of curd rice or a piece of bread, to eat the garlic with
a toothbrush and toothpaste
a clock, and a notebook page for the scores

schedule.what: One person eats raw garlic. The other scores the smell of their breath five times over two hours.

activities.record: A table with five rows: before eating, 5 minutes after, just after brushing, 1 hour after and 2 hours after. Write a smell score from 0 to 3 in each row.
activities.context: In this activity one person eats a little raw garlic. A second person smells their breath before and after brushing, and again one and two hours later.

setup.art: A grown-up eating a spoon of curd rice with chopped raw garlic on top, while a child holds a notebook.
setup.caption: 1. One person eats a small chopped clove of raw garlic.

setup.art: The grown-up brushing her teeth and tongue at a basin.
setup.caption: 2. Five minutes later the eater brushes teeth and tongue well.

setup.art: The child, a hand's width away, sniffing as the grown-up breathes out through her mouth.
setup.caption: 3. The sniffer scores the breath from 0 to 3, five times in two hours.

flow.do: Choose the eater: a grown-up, or the child if they like garlic. The other person is the sniffer. The sniffer smells the eater's breath from a hand's width away and writes a score from 0 to 3.
flow.say: One of us eats raw garlic, and the other is the sniffer. First, score the breath now, before any garlic. Zero means no garlic smell. Three means very strong.
flow.kid: Choose the eater and the sniffer. Score the breath before the garlic.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Garlic Breath Test. You score a person's breath before they eat raw garlic.

flow.do: The eater eats the chopped garlic with curd rice or bread. Five minutes later the sniffer scores the breath. Ask what brushing will do, and why.
flow.say: Score the breath now. Next, the eater will brush teeth and tongue very well. Will the garlic smell be gone after brushing? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Score the breath after the garlic. Will brushing remove the smell? Why?
flow.parent: Raw garlic is sharp. A small clove on curd rice is enough. Anyone who dislikes it should be the sniffer.
flow.context: In this step of the Garlic Breath Test you score the breath after raw garlic. You guess what brushing will do.

flow.do: The eater brushes teeth and tongue for two minutes and rinses. The sniffer scores the breath at once. They score it again 1 hour and 2 hours after the garlic was eaten.
flow.say: The mouth is clean now. Score the breath. We will score it again one hour and two hours after the garlic.
flow.kid: Score the breath after brushing. Score again at 1 hour and 2 hours.
flow.wait: Score again 1 hour and 2 hours after the garlic was eaten
flow.context: In this step of the Garlic Breath Test you score the breath just after brushing. You score it again 1 hour and 2 hours after the garlic.

flow.do: Look at the five scores. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they found, and why. Then read them the note below.
flow.say: Look at the five scores. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. The mouth was clean. So where was the smell coming from?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you found. Say why.

ask.q: The mouth was brushed clean. Where could the smell be coming from?
good: From deeper inside, such as the lungs.
The garlic went into the blood.
The blood carried it to the lungs.

flow.parent: In most people the smell is weaker after brushing but still clear, and it lasts for hours. The reason: one smelly chemical from garlic passes from the gut into the blood. The body breaks it down slowly. Until then it leaves through the lungs with each breath, and a little leaves through the skin. In 1999 Fabrizis Suarez and his team in the United States measured this in people's breath.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Garlic Breath Test. You say why the garlic smell stayed on the breath after the teeth were brushed.

activities.title: What Sweat Leaves Behind: the salt plate

materials.item: salt, a quarter of a teaspoon
drinking water, 2 tablespoons
dark or steel plates
a teaspoon and a small bowl
a fan or a sunny window sill

schedule.what: Dry a spoonful of salty water and a spoonful of plain water. Play until you sweat, and taste a drop.

activities.record: Draw the two plates after they have dried. Write what was left on each. Write what your own sweat tasted like.
activities.context: In this activity you let a spoonful of salty water dry on a plate. It shows what dried sweat leaves behind. Then you taste a drop of your own sweat.

setup.art: Two steel plates side by side under a ceiling fan, each with a thin wet patch, one labelled salty and one labelled plain.
setup.caption: 1. Spread 1 teaspoon of salty water on one plate and 1 teaspoon of plain water on the other.

setup.art: A child skipping with a rope indoors, with drops of sweat on her forehead.
setup.caption: 2. While the plates dry, skip or dance for ten minutes.

setup.art: The two plates after drying, one with a white crust and one almost clean.
setup.caption: 3. Look at both plates when they are dry.

flow.do: Dissolve a quarter teaspoon of salt in 2 tablespoons of drinking water. Spread 1 teaspoon of it thinly on one plate. Spread 1 teaspoon of plain drinking water on the other plate. Put both under a fan or in the sun.
flow.say: This salty water is our pretend sweat. It is much saltier than real sweat, so that we can see the result. What will be on each plate when the water has dried? Why?
flow.kid: Spread salty water on one plate. Spread plain water on the other. Guess what will be left.
flow.parent: Under a fan the thin patches dry in one to two hours. In the sun they dry faster.
flow.context: This is the first step of What Sweat Leaves Behind. You spread salty water and plain water on two plates to dry.

flow.do: Your child skips, dances or does star jumps for about ten minutes, until their forehead is damp. They touch a drop of sweat on the upper lip with the tip of the tongue.
flow.say: Move until your forehead is damp. Now taste one drop from your upper lip. What does it taste of?
flow.kid: Skip or dance until you sweat. Taste one drop. What is the taste?
flow.parent: On a cool day a child may not sweat in ten minutes. Then do this step after outdoor play on another day.
flow.context: In this step of What Sweat Leaves Behind you play until you sweat. Then you taste a drop of your own sweat.

flow.do: When both plates are dry, look at them together. Rub a finger across each. Talk about the questions below.
flow.say: Look at the two plates. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. The water has gone. Where did it go, and why did the salt stay?
flow.kid: Look at both plates. What is left? Where did the water go?
flow.wait: Wait until both plates are dry, about one to two hours under a fan

ask.q: When sweat dries on your skin, what leaves and what stays?
good: The water goes into the air.
The salt stays on the skin.

check.q: Sweat dries on a dark cap and leaves a white line. What is the white line?
check.why: Water evaporates, which means it turns into a gas and goes into the air. Salt cannot do that, so it stays. If you chose 'dried water', remember that water leaves nothing behind when it dries.

flow.parent: The salty plate has a white crust. The plain plate is almost clean, with perhaps a faint ring from minerals in the water. Sweat's main job is cooling. The salt and the trace of urea in it are a small extra way out.
flow.context: This is the last step of What Sweat Leaves Behind. You compare the dried plate of salty water with the dried plate of plain water.

projects.title: The Salt Hunt: how much salt is in our packets?

materials.item: food packets from your kitchen, such as chips, mixture, biscuits, instant noodles, pickle and bread
a notebook page and a pencil
salt, 1 level teaspoon, and a small plate

schedule.what: Find the sodium on six packets and put the packets in order.
Work out the salt in the amount you really eat, and compare it with one teaspoon.

projects.record: A table with one row for each packet. Write its name, the sodium in 100 grams, the grams you would eat at one time and the salt in that amount.
projects.context: In this two-day project you read the labels on six food packets. You work out how much salt each one gives your kidneys to deal with.

setup.art: Six food packets in a row on a kitchen counter, turned to show the printed nutrition tables on their backs.
setup.caption: 1. Collect six packets. Find the word 'sodium' in each nutrition table.

setup.art: A child writing numbers from a packet into a notebook table.
setup.caption: 2. Write down the sodium in 100 grams. Put the packets in order.

setup.art: One level teaspoon of salt on a small plate, beside a packet of chips and a notebook with sums.
setup.caption: 3. Work out the salt in what you eat. Compare it with one teaspoon of salt.

flow.do: Day 1. Collect six packets. On each one, find the nutrition table and the line for sodium. Write the milligrams of sodium in 100 grams. Put the six packets in a row, from least sodium to most.
flow.say: Salt is made of sodium and chlorine. Labels count the sodium. Before we read them, guess which packet has the most. Then let us find out.
flow.kid: Find 'sodium' on six packets. Write the numbers. Line the packets up.

good: The biscuits are sweet but have salt too.
The noodles had the most.
The pickle is far above the rest.

flow.parent: Indian labels give sodium in milligrams for each 100 grams. Sweet biscuits and bread often surprise children. If you have fewer than six packets, use what you have.
flow.context: This is day 1 of the Salt Hunt. You read the sodium on six food packets and put them in order.

flow.do: Day 2. For each packet, estimate the grams eaten at one time. Work out the sodium in that amount. Multiply the sodium by 2 and a half to get the salt. Put 1 level teaspoon of salt on a plate to compare.
flow.say: To turn sodium into salt, multiply by two and a half. This teaspoon holds about 5 grams of salt. The World Health Organization says an adult should eat less than that in a day, and a child less still.
flow.kid: Work out the salt in each snack. Compare it with one teaspoon.
flow.wait: Do this the day after you read the labels

ask.q: After a very salty snack, what do your kidneys do with the extra salt?
good: They leave it in the urine.
They need water to carry it out, so I feel thirsty.

flow.parent: 1,000 milligrams make 1 gram. A 50-gram packet with 800 milligrams of sodium in 100 grams holds 400 milligrams of sodium. That is 1 gram of salt. Extra salt leaves through the kidneys with water, which is one reason salty food makes us thirsty.
flow.context: This is day 2 of the Salt Hunt. You work out the salt in the amount of each food you really eat.

challenges.title: Fast and Fine: a filter that is quick and still clears the water
challenges.problem: A tissue filter makes cloudy flour water clear, but it is slow. A tea strainer is fast, but the water stays cloudy. Your kidneys must filter finely and fast at the same time. Build a filter set-up that clears one tumbler of flour water. It must take less than half the time of a single tissue filter.
constraints: Do not squeeze or press the tissue. A squeezed tissue tears.
The filtered water must pass the spoon check: a spoon at the bottom of the bowl can be seen.
All of the tumbler must be filtered, not just the first few spoonfuls.
Time every try with a clock.
materials: one tumbler of water with 1 level teaspoon of atta stirred in, for each try
tea strainers, a colander or a sieve
a clock or a phone timer
general: Use a bigger filter. Line a colander or a large sieve with tissue, so that more tissue is at work.
Use several filters at once. Set up three tissue-lined strainers over three bowls and share the water among them.
Filter in two stages. Pour through a cloth first to catch the big grains, so that the tissue does not clog.
creative: Let the flour water stand for five minutes. Pour off the clearer top part and filter only that.
Fold the tissue into pleats like a paper fan, so that more tissue fits in one strainer.
Make many small filters from tissue held over tumblers with rubber bands, and pour a little into each.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own set-up. Draw it first. Time it with one tumbler of flour water, and do the spoon check. Write your time beside the time of the single tissue filter.
challenges.context: In this challenge you build a filter that clears flour water quickly. It is the problem each kidney solves with about a million tiny filters working side by side.

setup.art: A single tea strainer lined with tissue over a bowl, with cloudy water dripping slowly through and a clock beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Time one tissue filter with one tumbler of flour water.

setup.art: Three tissue-lined strainers over three bowls in a row, with a child pouring a little cloudy water into each.
setup.caption: 2. Build a set-up that should be faster. Time it.

setup.art: A child lowering a spoon into a bowl of clear water, with a notebook showing two times.
setup.caption: 3. Do the spoon check. Compare the two times.

flow.do: Stir 1 level teaspoon of atta into a tumbler of water. Line a tea strainer with two tissues. Start the clock and pour the water through, a little at a time. Stop the clock when the tumbler is empty and the dripping stops.
flow.say: First we time one tissue filter. Pour slowly and do not squeeze. Watch the drip. Does it stay fast, or does it slow down?
flow.kid: Pour flour water through one tissue filter. Time it.

ask.q: Why does the dripping slow down?
good: Flour blocks the holes in the tissue.
A layer of flour builds up on the tissue.

flow.parent: One tissue-lined strainer often takes 5 to 10 minutes for a tumbler. If it clogs completely, stop at 10 minutes and write 'more than 10'.
flow.context: This is the first step of Fast and Fine. You time how long one tissue filter takes to clear a tumbler of flour water.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Your child lists ideas for a faster set-up, then chooses one and draws it.
flow.say: The filter must stay just as fine, so the holes cannot be bigger. What else could you change? List every idea, then choose one.
flow.kid: Think of ways to go faster. Keep the holes small. Draw your best idea.
flow.context: In this step of Fast and Fine you plan a filter set-up. It must be faster than one tissue filter and just as fine.

flow.do: Your child builds the set-up. Stir a new tumbler of flour water. Start the clock, pour, and stop the clock when all of it is through. Do the spoon check.
flow.say: Build it and test it with a new tumbler of flour water. Was it faster than half the first time? Does it pass the spoon check?
flow.kid: Build your set-up. Time it. Do the spoon check.
flow.context: In this step of Fast and Fine you build your filter set-up. You time it with a tumbler of flour water.

flow.do: Compare the two times. Change one thing and try again if there is time. Then talk about the question below.
flow.say: Which change saved the most time? Each of your kidneys has about a million tiny filters. Why is that better than one big filter?
flow.kid: Compare the times. Why does a kidney have a million small filters?

ask.q: Why is a million tiny filters better than one big one?
good: Many filters working together are fast.
Each one can stay very fine.
If some are blocked, the others still work.

flow.parent: Praise a clear account of what slowed the filter as much as a fast time. Pressing harder is not the answer in the body either. High blood pressure over many years damages the kidney's filters.
flow.context: This is the last step of Fast and Fine. You compare your filter set-up with the kidney's million tiny filters.

items.p: What is excretion?
opts: Sending out wastes that cells have made
items.why: Excretion is the removal of wastes made by the body's own cells, such as carbon dioxide and urea.

items.p: The liver changes ammonia into a less harmful waste called ____.
items.why: Ammonia is left over when protein is broken down. The liver turns it into urea, and the kidneys remove the urea.

items.p: Match each thing to its way out of the body.
items.why: A gas leaves by the lungs. A waste dissolved in the blood leaves by the kidneys. Sweat leaves by the skin. Food that was never digested stays in the gut and leaves as stool.

items.p: Your kidneys are low in your belly, at the front.
items.why: False. The kidneys are in the back, just under the lowest ribs. The bladder is low in the belly.

items.p: Put these in order, to show the path of urine out of the body.
items.why: Urine is made in the kidney. It flows down the ureter, waits in the bladder and leaves by the urethra.

items.p: Which of these is too big to pass through the kidney's filter?
items.why: Water, salt and urea are tiny dissolved particles. A red blood cell is a whole cell, far bigger than the holes.

items.p: Sort these. Does each one pass the kidney's filter, or is it held back?
items.why: The filter sorts only by size. Small dissolved particles pass. Cells and large proteins are held back.

items.p: Tissue paper can filter dissolved salt out of water.
items.why: False. Dissolved salt is made of particles far smaller than the holes in tissue. In the Three Filters Test the liquid stayed salty after every filter.

items.p: Explain in two sentences why the kidneys must take things back after filtering.
items.a: The filter lets useful things, such as water, salt and sugar, pass out of the blood with the wastes. The body needs them, so the tubes take them back and leave the wastes.
items.why: A strong answer says that the filter cannot tell useful from harmful, and names something that is taken back.

items.p: An adult's kidneys filter 180 litres a day. About how much leaves as urine?
items.why: About 99 parts in every 100 are taken back. Only about 1 and a half litres leave as urine.

items.p: Urine is stored in a stretchy bag called the ____.
items.why: The bladder is a bag of muscle, low in the belly. It stretches as it fills.

items.p: Why is urine dark yellow after a hot afternoon with no water?
opts: The kidneys save water, so less water leaves
The kidneys make extra yellow colour
The sun changes the colour of blood
items.why: When the body is short of water, the tubes take back nearly all of it. The same wastes leave in less water, so the colour is stronger.

items.p: Draw a body outline. Add the two kidneys, the two ureters and the bladder, and label them.
items.a: Two bean shapes high in the back, one on each side of the backbone. A thin tube runs from each one down to a round bag low in the belly.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the kidneys under the lowest ribs, well above the bladder. It joins each kidney to the bladder with its own tube.
items.art: A blank outline of a child's body, seen from the front.

items.p: People disagree about how much water a child should drink.

views.says: Drink eight glasses every day, whether you are thirsty or not. Then you can never run short.
Drink when you are thirsty and look at your urine. Pale yellow means you have had enough.
In May, thirst comes too late. On hot days, drink before you go out to play.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason, using what you know about the kidneys. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. One reason is that the kidneys adjust the urine to what you drink. Another is that a child at play in the heat may notice thirst late.
items.why: Each view has something right in it. A strong answer uses the fact that healthy kidneys save or release water as needed, and takes hot days seriously.

items.p: Sweat dries on your skin. What goes into the air, and what stays behind?
items.a: The water evaporates and goes into the air. The salt cannot evaporate, so it stays on the skin.
items.why: A strong answer names both the water and the salt, and says that only the water turns into a gas.

items.p: A filter sorts things by one feature. Which one?
items.why: A filter is a set of holes. Things smaller than the holes pass, whatever their colour, taste or use.

items.p: The kidney's filter lets harmful urea through but stops useful sugar.
items.why: False. Both are small, so both pass through. The sugar is taken back afterwards, in the tube.

items.p: After tissue paper, the filtered tea in the Three Filters Test was still salty. Explain why.
items.a: Dissolved salt is made of particles far smaller than the holes in the tissue. So the salt passed through with the water.
items.why: A strong answer compares the size of the salt particles with the size of the holes.

items.p: Three of these pass through the kidney's filter. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: Water, salt and urea are small dissolved particles. A white blood cell is a whole cell and is held back.

items.p: An adult's kidneys filter 180 litres in 24 hours. How many litres do they filter in 12 hours?
items.why: 12 hours is half of 24 hours. Half of 180 is 90 litres.

items.p: Put these in order, to follow one particle of urea out of the body.
items: The liver makes it from ammonia
Blood carries it to a kidney
It is pushed through a filter
a: The liver makes it from ammonia
Blood carries it to a kidney
It is pushed through a filter
items.why: Urea is made in the liver and carried by the blood. It is filtered, left in the tube and stored in the bladder.

items.p: You drink two tumblers of water. What do the tubes in your kidneys do next?
items.why: Your blood has more water than it needs. The tubes take back less of it, so more leaves as pale urine.

items.p: Water goes from the stomach to the bladder through a tube of its own.
items.why: False. Water passes from the gut into the blood. The kidneys filter it out of the blood, and the ureters carry it to the bladder.

items.p: Sort these by their main way out of the body.
items: the salt in a white line on a cap
items.why: Things that turn into a gas leave by the lungs. Dissolved wastes leave by the kidneys. Sweat carries a little salt out through the skin.

items.p: A dry city plans to clean its used water, toilet water too, and make it drinking water again.

views.says: Our filters and tests make this water cleaner than river water. Every river already holds water that passed through animals, including humans.
I believe the tests. But I cannot forget where this water was. Let me choose.
Give the cleaned water to our fields first. Crops need the urea and the salts that you work so hard to remove.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason, using what you know about filters and wastes. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. One reason is that filters and other steps can remove dissolved wastes, as kidneys do. Another is that urea feeds plants.
items.why: Each view has something right in it. A strong answer uses what filters can and cannot remove, and takes people's feelings seriously.

items.p: Label three parts of this nephron: the glomerulus, the cup around it, and the tube.
a: The glomerulus: the ball of thin blood vessels that filters the blood
The cup: it collects the filtered liquid
The tube: it takes back water, salt and sugar
items.why: Filtering happens at the ball. Taking back happens along the tube. What is left at the end of the tube is urine.
items.art: A large simple drawing of one nephron: a ball of looped vessels inside a cup, joined to a long winding tube, with three blank label lines.

items.p: A person takes a new medicine. Explain how the kidneys remove what is left of it.
items.a: What is left of the medicine is small, so it passes the filter. Nothing in the tube takes it back. So it stays in the liquid and leaves in the urine.
items.why: A strong answer says that the kidney does not need to recognise the medicine. It only takes back what the body needs.

items.p: Why does garlic breath last after the teeth are brushed?
opts: A garlic chemical leaves through the lungs
items.why: A smelly chemical from garlic passes from the gut into the blood. It leaves through the lungs for hours.

items.p: The messenger chemical that tells the kidneys to save water is called ____.
items.why: The brain sends out more ADH when the body is short of water. The tubes then take back more water.

items.p: Why can a person not clean their blood by sweating in a hot room?
items.a: Sweat is almost all water, with a little salt and only a trace of urea. The kidneys remove far more waste. Sweating mostly removes water, which the person must then drink again.
items.why: A strong answer says what sweat is made of, and compares it with what the kidneys remove.

items.p: Does a cloth folded into 8 layers filter flour water better than one layer? Plan a fair test.
items.a: Make one batch of flour water and stir it before each pour. Pour the same amount through one layer and through eight layers. Use the same cloth and the same check, such as the spoon check. Change only the number of layers.
items.why: A strong answer changes one thing only and keeps the mixture and the amount the same. It names how the result will be judged.

items.p: A urine test finds protein. What does this most likely mean?
opts: Damaged filters are letting big particles through
The person ate too much dal
The person drank too little water
items.why: Large proteins are normally held back by the filter. Protein in the urine suggests that the filter has been hurt.

items.p: A urine test finds sugar. What does this most likely mean?
opts: The blood holds too much sugar to take back
The filter has stopped the sugar
items.why: Sugar always passes the filter. The tubes take it back, but only up to a limit. Sugar in the urine is a sign of too much sugar in the blood, as in diabetes.

items.p: A person with one healthy kidney can live a full life.
items.why: True. One healthy kidney is enough to clean the blood. The kidney that stays grows larger and filters more.

items.p: Explain how a dialysis machine uses the same idea as the Three Filters Test.
items.a: The blood flows past a thin sheet with very small holes. Small wastes such as urea pass through the holes into a bath of liquid. Blood cells and large proteins are too big, so they stay in the blood.
items.why: A strong answer says that the sheet sorts by size, and names one thing that passes and one that stays.

items.p: Match each part to its job.
pairs: Takes back water, salt and sugar
items.why: The liver prepares the waste. The glomerulus and the tube do the two steps of cleaning. The ureter and the bladder only carry and store the urine.

items.p: One tissue filter clears a tumbler in 9 minutes. Three such filters share the water. How many minutes do they take?
items.why: Each filter gets one third of the water, so each takes one third of the time. 9 divided by 3 is 3 minutes.

items.p: One kidney has been given, and three people are waiting for it.

views.says: It should go to the person whose body it matches best. Then it will last the longest.

views.who: A nurse on the dialysis ward
views.says: It should go to the person who has waited longest. Waiting is hard, and a queue is fair.
It should go to the child. A child has the most years ahead.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. A good answer may combine them, for example the best match among those who have waited longest.
items.why: This is a real question that hospitals must answer. There is no single right view. A strong answer gives a reason and treats the other views fairly.

items.p: The urine in a healthy bladder has no living microbes in it at all.
items.why: False. For a long time doctors thought so. In 2014 scientists using better tests found living bacteria in the bladders of healthy people.

items.p: Some people say that sweating removes toxins. What would you measure to test this claim?
items.a: Measure how much of one named toxin is in a person's sweat in a day. Measure how much of it leaves in the urine in a day. Compare the two amounts.
items.why: A strong answer names something to measure and compares sweat with urine. Scientists who did this found that sweat removes very little.

items.p: Draw one nephron. Use one colour of arrow for filtering and another colour for taking back.
items.a: A ball inside a cup with arrows going out of the ball into the cup. A long tube leaves the cup, with arrows going from the tube back into a blood vessel beside it.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the two steps in two different places: filtering at the ball and taking back along the tube.
items.art: A blank box with the words 'filtering' and 'taking back' and two small squares to colour as a key.

items.p: Most children sleep ten hours without a toilet visit. What is the best explanation?
opts: The kidneys make less urine at night
The kidneys stop working at night
The bladder doubles in size at night
Cells make no waste at night
items.why: At night the tubes take back more water, so less urine reaches the bladder. The kidneys never stop, and cells make waste all night.

items.p: Cells make the gas ____ ____ when they use food for energy.
items.why: Carbon dioxide is made in every working cell. The blood carries it to the lungs.

items.p: Why does the liver change ammonia into urea?
opts: Ammonia is a poison, and urea is much safer
Ammonia is too big for the kidney's filter
items.why: Even a little ammonia in the blood harms the brain. Urea can travel safely in the blood until the kidneys remove it.

items.p: A stool is mostly undigested food. Why is that food not called a waste made by cells?
items.a: The food passed along the tube of the gut. It never entered the blood or a cell, so no cell made it.
items.why: A strong answer says that excretion means removing what cells have made. Undigested food was never taken into the cells.

quiz.p: Which three organs are the main ways out for the body's wastes?
quiz.why: The lungs remove carbon dioxide. The kidneys remove dissolved wastes. The skin lets out sweat.

quiz.p: Which waste leaves the body through the lungs?
quiz.why: Carbon dioxide is a gas. It passes from the blood into the air in the lungs, and you breathe it out.
The liver changes poisonous ammonia into urea. The kidneys then remove the urea from the blood.

quiz.p: Why must wastes leave the body?
opts: They would build up and poison the cells
They take up too much room
They make the body too heavy
quiz.why: Cells make waste all the time. If it stayed in the blood, it would reach harmful levels within days.

quiz.p: What do the kidneys make urine from?
opts: From the air in the lungs
From water stored in the bladder
quiz.why: Blood flows into the kidneys, and the kidneys filter it. Urine is what is left after the useful parts are taken back.

quiz.p: What does the kidney's filter hold back?
quiz.why: The filter sorts by size. Cells and large proteins are too big for its holes. Water, salt, sugar and urea pass through.

quiz.p: After the blood is filtered, what does the tube of a nephron do?
opts: Takes back water, salt and sugar
quiz.why: The tube returns what the body needs to the blood. What it does not take back becomes urine.

quiz.p: A kidney must recognise each waste before it can remove it.
quiz.why: False. Everything small passes the filter. The kidney takes back what the body needs, and the rest leaves, whatever it is.

quiz.p: In the Three Filters Test, which things passed through the tissue paper?
opts: The salt and the tea colour
quiz.why: Dissolved salt and dissolved tea colour are far smaller than the holes in a tissue. Leaves and flour grains are bigger.

quiz.p: What is urine mostly made of?
quiz.why: Urine is about 95 parts water in every 100. Urea, salts and other wastes are dissolved in it.

opts: A waste made from old red blood cells
quiz.why: When old red blood cells are broken down, a yellow waste called urobilin is left. The kidneys send it out.

quiz.p: What is the main job of sweat?
opts: To remove most of the urea
quiz.why: Sweat cools you as its water evaporates. It carries only a little salt and a trace of urea.

quiz.p: What does a dialysis machine do?
opts: Cleans the blood when the kidneys cannot
Pumps blood when the heart cannot
quiz.why: In dialysis, blood flows past a sheet with tiny holes. Wastes pass out through the holes, and the cleaned blood returns to the body.

applications: Dialysis machines clean the blood of people whose kidneys have failed. The blood flows past a thin sheet with tiny holes, and urea passes out through the holes.
A urine test at a clinic can find illness early. Sugar in the urine points to diabetes, and protein points to damaged filters.
Many home water purifiers push water through a sheet with very fine holes. Like a kidney's filter, the sheet needs pressure to work.
On the International Space Station, machines clean the crew's urine and sweat and turn them back into drinking water.
Traffic police use a breath test to find drivers who have drunk alcohol. It works because alcohol leaves the blood through the lungs.
Farmers spread urea on their fields as food for crops. Factories make this urea from the nitrogen in air.

open_questions.q: Why can humans not grow new nephrons after birth?
open_questions.why_open: A baby is born with all the nephrons they will ever have. Zebrafish grow new ones all their lives. Scientists do not yet know how to make a human kidney do this.

open_questions.q: Can a kidney grown in a laboratory be made to work in a person?
open_questions.why_open: In 2015 Melissa Little and her team in Australia grew tiny kidney-like organs from human cells. They have nephrons, but no way yet to carry urine out or to connect to a blood supply.

open_questions.q: Can a pig's kidney work for years inside a human?
open_questions.why_open: In 2024 surgeons in the United States placed kidneys from specially bred pigs into living patients. Nobody yet knows how long such a kidney can last.

open_questions.q: Why are so many farm workers in some hot places losing their kidneys?
open_questions.why_open: Many farm workers have kidney disease with no known cause. This is seen in the Uddanam area of Andhra Pradesh, in Sri Lanka and in Central America. Heat, too little water and something in the water or soil are all suspected.

open_questions.q: How much water does a person really need each day?
open_questions.why_open: It depends on body size, weather, food and work. Studies give a wide range, and no single number fits everyone.

maths.problem: An adult's kidneys filter 180 litres a day. The watery part of an adult's blood is about 3 litres. About how many times a day is it filtered?
maths.explain: 180 divided by 3 is 60. The same 3 litres pass through the filters again and again, about 60 times in a day.
maths.context: In Ninety-Nine Back you took 2 teaspoons from a litre, to show how little of the filtered liquid becomes urine.
maths.why_maths: Dividing shows that the kidneys do not filter the blood once. They clean the same liquid many times a day.

maths.problem: An adult's kidneys filter 180 litres a day and pass 1 and a half litres as urine. How many litres are taken back? Is that more or less than 99 parts in 100?
maths.answer: 178 and a half litres are taken back. That is a little more than 99 parts in 100.
maths.explain: 180 minus 1 and a half is 178 and a half. One part in 100 of 180 litres is 1.8 litres. The urine is less than that, so more than 99 parts are taken back.
maths.context: In Ninety-Nine Back you measured how little of the liquid filtered by the kidneys leaves as urine.
maths.why_maths: Working out the share shows that taking back, not throwing out, is most of a kidney's work.

maths.problem: In the Three Filters Test, the strainer stopped leaves only. The cloth stopped leaves and some flour. The tissue stopped leaves and nearly all the flour. A fourth filter has even finer holes than tissue. What might it stop? Could any filter with holes stop salt?
maths.answer: It might stop the last of the flour. A filter could stop dissolved salt only if its holes were smaller than a salt particle.
maths.explain: Each finer filter stopped smaller things than the one before. Dissolved salt particles are thousands of times smaller than the holes in tissue. The pattern says that a filter stops whatever is bigger than its holes.
maths.context: In the Three Filters Test you poured salty tea with flour in it through a strainer, a cloth and a tissue.
maths.why_maths: Following the pattern from one filter to the next lets you predict a filter you have not tested.

maths.problem: On a water afternoon, two tumblers were drunk at 3:00. The toilet visits were at 3:45, 4:20 and 5:10. How long was it until the first visit? Which gap between visits was longest, and what might that show?
maths.answer: 45 minutes until the first visit. The longest gap was the last one, 50 minutes. It suggests that the extra water was nearly gone.
maths.explain: From 3:00 to 3:45 is 45 minutes. From 3:45 to 4:20 is 35 minutes. From 4:20 to 5:10 is 50 minutes. As the extra water leaves, the bladder fills more slowly.
maths.context: In After Two Tumblers you drink two tumblers of water at 3 o'clock and record every toilet visit. These times are made up.
maths.why_maths: Working out the gaps shows how quickly the kidneys answered and when they finished.

maths.problem: A packet of chips weighs 50 grams. Its label says 800 milligrams of sodium in 100 grams. Salt is 2 and a half times the sodium. How much salt is in the packet? How many such packets hold 5 grams of salt?
maths.answer: 1 gram of salt in one packet. Five packets hold 5 grams.
maths.explain: 50 grams is half of 100 grams, so the packet has 400 milligrams of sodium. 400 times 2 and a half is 1,000 milligrams, which is 1 gram of salt. 5 times 1 gram is 5 grams, about one teaspoon.
maths.context: In the Salt Hunt you read the sodium on food packets. You work out the salt your kidneys must deal with.
maths.why_maths: The label hides the salt in two steps: sodium, and 100 grams. Multiplying brings out the amount you really eat.

maths.problem: One tissue filter clears a tumbler of flour water in 8 minutes. How long would 2 such filters take, sharing the water? And 4 filters? A kidney has about a million filters. What does the pattern tell you?
maths.answer: 2 filters take 4 minutes. 4 filters take 2 minutes. With a million filters, even very slow, fine filters clear a lot of liquid quickly.
maths.explain: Twice as many filters halve the time. 8 divided by 2 is 4, and 8 divided by 4 is 2. The time keeps falling as filters are added, and the filters stay just as fine.
maths.context: In Fast and Fine you try to clear flour water quickly without making the holes in the filter bigger.
maths.why_maths: The pattern shows why the kidney is built from many tiny filters and not one large one.

maths.problem: A nine-year-old's bladder holds about 300 millilitres. By day the kidneys send it about 40 millilitres each hour. In how many hours would it fill? Most children sleep 10 hours without a toilet visit. How can that be?
maths.answer: It would fill in about 7 and a half hours. The kidneys must make less urine at night.
maths.explain: 300 divided by 40 is 7 and a half. Ten hours of sleep is longer than that. So the night rate must be lower than 40 millilitres an hour, and it is. At night the tubes take back more water.
maths.context: In Find Your Kidneys you drew the path of urine from the kidneys to the bladder. These numbers are rounded.
maths.why_maths: When a sum disagrees with what really happens, the gap points to something the sum left out.

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, many doctors thought a kidney made urine the way a gland makes spit. On this idea, the kidney's cells picked each waste out of the blood and pushed it into the urine. In 1842 the English doctor William Bowman drew the kidney's tiny tubes under a microscope. Each tube began as a cup around a ball of blood vessels. In the 1840s the German scientist Carl Ludwig proposed that the ball is a filter. He said that the push of the blood drives water and small particles through it. The tube then takes most of them back. Few people accepted this, and the argument lasted eighty years. In 1924, in Philadelphia, Joseph Wearn and Alfred Newton Richards settled it. They worked on a frog who had been put to sleep. They slid a glass pipette, finer than a hair, into one cup and drew out a tiny drop. The drop held salt and sugar, as blood does, but no protein. The urine in the frog's bladder held no sugar. So sugar had passed the filter, and the tube had taken it back.
how_we_found_out.who: William Bowman in England, Carl Ludwig in Germany, and Joseph Wearn and Alfred Newton Richards in the United States
how_we_found_out.when: Bowman published his drawings in 1842. Ludwig proposed filtering in the 1840s. Wearn and Richards published their frog experiment in 1924.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That the kidney's cells pick each waste out of the blood and push it into the urine. Wearn and Richards showed that the liquid just past the filter holds sugar and salt, like blood without its proteins. The kidney filters first and takes back afterwards.
how_we_found_out.art: A laboratory bench of the 1920s with a microscope, and a very fine glass pipette held in a brass stand above a small dish.

roots.context: In this unit you poured salty tea through three filters and learned how the kidneys clean the blood. Here we ask what it means to clean something, and where a waste goes after it leaves you.

deep_truth.truth: In the Three Filters Test, every filter let the salt and the tea colour pass with the water. The filters in your kidneys also let salt, sugar and urea out of the blood together. Then the kidneys take back the water, salt and sugar that your body needs. Whatever they do not take back leaves as urine, even a waste your body has never met.
deep_truth.habit: We think of cleaning as finding the dirt and taking it out. To do that, the cleaner must know every kind of dirt. The kidneys clean the blood by knowing what the body needs, and they let everything else go.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Three Filters Test the tissue held back the leaves and the flour. The liquid stayed brown and salty. In 1924 Wearn and Richards found sugar in the liquid just past a frog's filter. They found none in the frog's urine. A healthy person's urine holds no sugar, though sugar passes the filter all day.

three.who_am_i: About half the water in your body is replaced every week or two. Your body keeps its shape while the water and salt in it keep changing.
three.what_is_life: A living body takes things in, keeps what it needs for a while and lets the rest go. A body that stopped letting go would die within days.
three.what_is_this_world: There is no "away" to throw things to, because everything stays inside the same world. The urea and the water that you let go are taken up by soil bacteria, plants, rivers and clouds.

roots.thread: The water in your urine was rain, river water and tap water before it was blood. The nitrogen in your urea was in the protein of a dal seed. Before that it was in the soil and the air. After the urea leaves you, bacteria in the soil turn the urea into food for plants. So the same atoms pass through cloud, plant, animal and soil in turn. The teacher Thich Nhat Hanh called this interbeing, which means that each thing is made of other things.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka teaches his son Shvetaketu that food, once eaten, becomes three things. The coarsest part becomes stool, the middle part becomes flesh and the finest part becomes mind. Water, once drunk, also becomes three things: urine, blood and breath.
teachings.link: This is a very old attempt to follow what the body keeps and what it lets go. Science agrees that the body sorts what it takes in. It differs on the details. Urine is made from the blood, by the kidneys.

teachings.teaching: A rose becomes garbage within a few weeks, and garbage becomes compost that feeds the next rose. A good gardener looks at a rose and sees the garbage, and looks at garbage and sees a rose.
teachings.link: Urea leaves your body as a waste and reaches a plant as food. So the word 'waste' only describes what a thing is for one body at one moment. For another living being, the same thing can be food.

science.text: Atoms are not destroyed in the body. Every atom of nitrogen that leaves in urea goes on to the soil, the water or the air. Plants take up many of them.

In 1953 the kidney scientist Homer Smith wrote about what decides what the blood is made of. He said it is decided mostly by what the kidneys keep, and less by what goes in through the mouth. He also argued that this steady inner liquid allowed animals to leave the sea for the land.

other_view.who: Carl Ludwig and other scientists of the 1840s, and many scientists today
other_view.view: There is no choosing or knowing in a kidney. The push of the blood drives liquid through holes. Pumps in the tube's cells move particles by the rules of physics and chemistry. On this view, words such as 'keeps' and 'needs' are only a short way to describe a mechanism.

practice.title: One breath out, one sip in

ask: Your kidneys do not need to know what a waste is. They need to know what your body needs. How might a kidney know that?
The urea that leaves you today may be part of a tomato plant next year. When did it stop being yours?
In the story What Fell Through the Sieve, Yazhini threw away things she could not name. Could something useful have been among them? Could a kidney make the same mistake?

playtest: Read through as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, step by step, but not yet done at home. The Three Filters Test (core) needs tea leaves, salt, atta, a tea strainer, a thin cotton cloth, paper tissues and three small steel bowls. It takes about 35 minutes. A grown-up pours the hot water, and the tea must cool before the child handles it. The expected result is that the strainer stops the leaves, the cloth stops some flour and the tissue stops nearly all the flour. All three bowls stay brown and salty. The tissue is slow and may clog, so the step says to stop after 5 minutes. The third bowl may still be a little hazy, and the cloth bowl may look much like the strainer bowl. The steps say to write what is really seen. The child tastes one drop from each bowl, so use drinking water and clean things. Find Your Kidneys and Ninety-Nine Back (both core) need only a pencil, a litre bottle and a teaspoon. After Two Tumblers takes two afternoons at home. Bodies differ: a child who was short of water before the test will pass less, and the note says so. Two tumblers are a safe amount, and no more should be given. The Garlic Breath Test needs someone willing to eat a small raw clove, and it is skipped if nobody is. The salt plate dries in one to two hours under a fan, and plain tap water may leave a faint ring. On a cool day the child may not sweat in ten minutes. In Fast and Fine, one tissue filter may take 5 to 10 minutes for a tumbler, so the target is half of your own first time. The Salt Hunt needs packets with a nutrition table. Facts to treat with care: the figures of 180 litres filtered and 1 and a half litres of urine are for adults and are rounded. The bladder size for a nine-year-old, about 300 millilitres, and the 40 millilitres an hour are rounded. The number of sweat glands is given as 2 to 4 million. Kolff's first survivor was treated in 1945. The salt in dried sweat is real, but real sweat is far weaker than the salty water used on the plate. The idea that blood salt is left over from an ancient sea is marked as debated. The Chandogya Upanishad passage is given as a paraphrase. The three videos have no address yet.
